description: Hi! I'm Sithumini, a Software Engineering undergraduate passionate about web development, AI, data visualization, and creative technology. For NASA Space Apps, I'm exploring the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge and looking for curious, creative teammates interested in space science, NASA data, GIS/mapping, UI/UX, AI/ML, or presentations. You don't need to be an expert—just bring your ideas, skills, and enthusiasm to collaborate and build something meaningful.
summary:
MARSCOPE is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-support app built to help crews and mission planners examine surface locations and organize exploration. Its Marswalk map brings together available planetary imagery, terrain information, named features, crew reports, and points of interest. Users can inspect Gale Crater and other mapped regions, review nearby observations, and explore route-planning, hazard, survival, and crew-tracking tools.

The project addresses the challenge of turning scattered Mars data into a localized view that can support planning a surface excursion. It combines available NASA and planetary datasets with clear source and readiness information, and uses visibly labeled demo data where live mission data is unavailable. This distinction matters: Mars terrain measurements and crew reports can inform exploration, but they do not automatically establish that a place is safe. MARSCOPE provides an accessible foundation for exploring the data and identifying what is known, missing, or still needs validation before operational use.
details:
Project details

MARSCOPE is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-support application. Its Marswalk map lets users explore surface locations, inspect planetary imagery and terrain information, view named features and crew reports, and select points of interest. Supporting tools cover route planning, hazard and risk assessment, crew tracking, survival resources, collaborative mapping, and mission reports.

The app connects available planetary data and services to location-based views. Where live sources or validated models are unavailable, it can show clearly labeled demo data. Those examples help people explore the interface without presenting simulated values as real Mars observations or operational predictions.

Benefits and intended impact: MARSCOPE brings exploration context into one place, helping users see what information is available around a location and what is still missing. The intended impact is to make planetary data easier to explore and support better-informed planning for future Mars surface excursions.

Tools and technologies: The project uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS, and Resium for the interactive maps; Python and FastAPI for backend APIs and geospatial processing; and NASA and planetary data services for scientific context. The development setup uses standard computers and web browsers; no specialized hardware is required.

Creative approach: MARSCOPE combines a 3D Mars globe with map layers, location-aware context, and mission-support features. It also communicates data provenance and limitations in the experience, so users can distinguish live or sourced information from illustrative demos.

Factors considered: The team considered planetary coordinate systems, dataset coverage and resolution, source availability, map readability, and the difference between terrain observations, hazard classifications, and mission-risk predictions. Demo data is marked as simulated, while missing real data and model readiness are shown explicitly.
